paragraphs.heading: A turbine under water
paragraphs.text: A tidal stream generator is a machine that takes energy out of moving masses of water, tides in particular. It is often called a tidal energy converter. Some types work very much like wind turbines placed under water, which is why they are often called tidal turbines. The idea was first conceived during the oil crisis of the 1970s.

paragraphs.heading: Why water beats air
paragraphs.text: A tidal turbine draws on water currents much as a wind turbine draws on air currents. Water has about 800 times the density of air. Because of that, one generator can give significant power at tidal flow velocities that are low compared with similar wind speeds. Power varies with the density of the medium and with the cube of the velocity. As a result, water moving at nearly one-tenth the speed of wind gives the same power for a turbine system of the same size.

paragraphs.heading: Where they can work
paragraphs.text: In practice this limits tidal turbines to places where the tide runs at two knots (1 m/s) or more. In faster seawater flows of between two and three meters per second, a tidal turbine can typically reach four times the energy for each unit of rotor swept area that a wind turbine of similar rated power can. Tidal power generation has four main forms, and of these tidal stream generators are the cheapest and the least ecologically damaging.

paragraphs.heading: Many designs, no winner
paragraphs.text: There is a large variety of designs, and no standard one has come out as the clear winner. The European Marine Energy Centre counts six principal types. They are turbines with a horizontal axis, turbines with a vertical axis, oscillating hydrofoils, venturi devices, Archimedes’ screws and tidal kites. Several prototypes have shown promise. None, however, has operated commercially for long enough to establish its performance and its rate of return on investment.

paragraphs.heading: The first on the grid
paragraphs.text: The HS300 turbine was connected to the grid on November 13, 2003, while still a prototype. Its reported capacity was 300 kW. No tidal turbine anywhere had delivered to the grid before it. Its submerged structure weighed 120 tonnes and sat on gravity footings of 200 tonnes. It had three blades of plastic reinforced with glass fibre, each 10 metres from hub to tip. The device turned at 7 rpm.

paragraphs.heading: Strong currents, broken blades
paragraphs.text: Strong currents are hard on the machines. In April 2007 Verdant Power started a prototype project in the East River in New York City, between Queens and Roosevelt Island. The United States had not had a major tidal-power project before this one. The strong currents made the design difficult. Blades broke on both the 2006 and the 2007 prototypes, and new reinforced turbines were installed in September 2008.

paragraphs.heading: A floating prototype
paragraphs.text: One prototype floated. The SR2000 was a 2MW floating turbine that Orbital Marine Power developed in Scotland, and it was operated at the European Marine Energy Centre in Orkney from 2016. In 12 months of continuous testing it produced 3,200 MWhs of electricity. In September 2018 it was taken away to make room for the production model, the Orbital O2, which was completed in 2021.
